criteria_quotes: Unicompartmental knee arthroplasty using Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved devices is considered medically necessary for members with advanced osteoarthritis or post-traumatic arthritis of the knee affecting only a single compartment (medial, lateral or patellofemoral), and who meet the following criteria (see also Additional Note):
Pain and functional disability that interferes with ADLs due to osteoarthritis or post-traumatic arthritis of the knee joint; and
Limited range of motion, crepitus, or effusion or swelling of knee joint on physical examination: and
Member must have intact, stable ligaments, in particular the anterior cruciate ligament; and
Patient’s knee arc of motion (full extension to full flexion) is not limited to 90 degrees or less; and

Radiographic evidence of moderate/severe osteoarthritis (i.e., Kellgren-Lawrence Grade 3 or 4) (see Appendix) affecting only a single (medial, lateral or patellofemoral) compartment of the knee joint; and

History of of unsuccessful conservative therapy (non-surgical medical management; 12 or 24 weeks depending on age/BMI) that is clearly addressed in the medical record (see Note Footnote3 ***) with at least half of the necessary conservative therapy consisting of formal physical therapy (in-person with a licensed physical therapist as opposed to home or virtual physical therapy). Physical therapy needs to be confirmed either by the actual PT notes, or by documentation in the member claims history. Conservative therapy may be inappropriate for severe osteoarthritis with bone-on-bone articulation in the weight-bearing portion of the joint (medial and/or lateral but not patello-femoral); and

Member has none of the following contraindications to unicompartmental knee arthroplasty: Previous proximal tibial osteotomy or distal femoral osteotomy; or Tibial or femoral shaft deformity; or Radiographic evidence of medial or lateral subluxation; or Flexion contracture greater than 15 degrees; or Varus deformity greater than 15 degrees (medial unicompartmental knee arthroplasty) or a valgus deformity greater than 20 degrees (lateral unicompartmental knee arthroplasty); or Inflammatory or crystalline arthropathy; or Subchondral bone loss due to large subchondral cysts or extensive focal osteonecrosis.

Member has none of the following absolute contraindications to joint replacement: Active infection of the joint or active systemic bacteremia that has not been totally eradicated; or Active skin infection (exception recurrent cutaneous staph infections) or open wound within the planned surgical site of the knee; or Corticosteroid injection into the joint within 12 weeks of the planned arthroplasty; or Vascular insufficiency, significant muscular atrophy of the leg, or neuromuscular disease severe enough to compromise implant stability or post-operative recovery or quadriplegia; or Osseous abnormalities that cannot be optimally managed and which would increase the likelihood of a poor surgical outcome (i.e., inadequate bone stock to support the implant); or Allergy to components of the implant (e.g., cobalt, chromium or alumina).
If member is diabetic, their hemoglobin A1C (HbA1c) should be less than 8 percent within 3 months prior to knee arthroplasty.
answer.submission_route: The appeal should be submitted in writing to the specific address or fax number printed on the denial letter (Notice of Adverse Benefit Determination) or on the back of the member's health plan ID card. Members may also file appeals online through the secure Aetna Member Portal, or call Aetna Member Services for guidance. Aetna's general commercial mailing address for appeals is: Aetna Provider Resolution Team, PO Box 14020, Lexington, KY 40512 (National Fax: 859-455-8650).
answer.how_to_obtain_criteria: The clinical criteria are publicly available online in Aetna's Clinical Policy Bulletin (CPB) 0660 at https://www.aetna.com/cpb/medical/data/600_699/0660.html. Alternatively, the patient can request a copy of the specific medical-necessity criteria applied to their determination by calling the Aetna Member Services department using the telephone number on the back of their member ID card.
answer.notes: CPT code 27446 covers unicompartmental knee arthroplasty (partial knee replacement). The policy notes that conservative therapy includes anti-inflammatory medications/analgesics, flexibility and muscle-strengthening exercises, activity modification, and supervised physical therapy. Relative contraindications to joint replacement under this policy include morbid obesity (BMI > 40) and age under 50, in which cases members should exhaust all nonsurgical treatment options before surgery is approved.

result.text: Knee Arthroplasty - Medical Clinical Policy Bulletins | Aetna --> Top Knee Arthroplasty Clinical Policy Bulletins Medical Clinical Policy Bulletins Print Share Number: 0660 Table Of Contents Policy Applicable CPT / HCPCS / ICD-10 Codes Background References Policy Scope of Policy This Clinical Policy Bulletin addresses knee arthroplasty. Note: Precertification may be required for select procedures and interventions. Use the CPT code search tool to see if precertification is required. Medical Necessity Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved total knee arthroplasty (TKA) prosthesis is considered medically necessary for adult members when the following criteria are met (see also Additional Note ): Member has advanced joint disease demonstrated by: Pain and functional disability that interferes with ADLs from injury due to osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, avascular necrosis, or post-traumatic arthritis of the knee joint; and Limited range of motion, crepitus, or effusion or swelling of knee joint on physical examination: and Member has any of the following: Radiographic evidence of moderate/severe osteoarthritis of knee joint (i.e., Kellgren-Lawrence Grade 3 or 4) (see Appendix ); or Radiographic evidence of avascular necrosis (osteonecrosis) of tibial or femoral condyle; or Radiographic evidence or rheumatoid arthritis (joint space narrowing); and History of unsuccessful conservative therapy (non-surgical medical management; 12 or 24 weeks depending on age/body mass index (BMI)) that is clearly addressed in the medical record (see Footnote1 Note* ). Conservative therapy may be inappropriate for severe osteoarthritis with bone-on-bone articulation in the weight-bearing portion of the joint (medial and/or lateral but not patello-femoral) or severe angular deformity, or for avascular necrosis with collapse of tibial or femoral condyle, or progressive flexion contracture. If conservative therapy is not appropriate, the medical record must clearly document why such approach is not reasonable; or Failure of a previous osteotomy with pain interfering with ADLs; or Distal femur or proximal tibia malunion by imaging with pain interfering with ADLs; Distal femur or proximal tibia fracture or nonunion; or Malignancy of the distal femur, proximal tibia, knee joint or adjacent soft tissues by imaging; or Failure of previous unicompartmental knee replacement with pain interfering with ADLs. Footnote1 *Note: Physical therapy needs to be confirmed either by the actual PT notes, or by documentation in the member claims history. Members with osteoarthritis, traumatic arthritis, or avascular necrosis should have at least 12 weeks of non-surgical treatment documented in the medical record (at least 24 weeks for persons with a relative contraindication) - with at least half of the necessary conservative therapy consisting of formal physical therapy (in-person with a licensed physical therapist as opposed to home or virtual physical therapy) in the past year, including all of the following, unless contraindicated: Anti-inflammatory medications or analgesics; and Flexibility and muscle strengthening exercises; and Activity modification; and Supervised physical therapy (in-person with a licensed physical therapist as opposed to home or virtual physical therapy; activities of daily living (ADLs) diminished despite completing a plan of care); and Assistive device use (required for persons with relative contraindications Footnote2 ** to joint replacement, optional for others); and Therapeutic injections into the knee (required for persons with relative contraindications Footnote2 ** to joint replacement, optional for others). Total joint replacement is considered not medically necessary in persons with any of the following absolute contraindications: Active infection of the joint or active systemic bacteremia that has not been totally eradicated; or Active skin infection (exception recurrent cutaneous staph infections) or open wound within the planned surgical site of the knee; or Corticosteroid injection into the joint within 12 weeks of the planned arthroplasty; or Vascular insufficiency, significant muscular atrophy of the leg, or neuromuscular disease severe enough to compromise implant stability or post-operative recovery or quadriplegia; or Osseous abnormalities that cannot be optimally managed and which would increase the likelihood of a poor surgical outcome (i.e., inadequate bone stock to support the implant); or Allergy to components of the implant (e.g., cobalt, chromium or alumina). For members with significant conditions or co-morbidities, the risk/benefit of total knee arthroplasty should be appropriately addressed in the medical record. Footnote2 ** Relative contraindications to joint replacement include the following: morbid obesity (BMI greater than 40), age less than 50 years). Members with relative contraindications should exhaust all nonsurgical treatment options. Revision or replacement of total knee arthroplasty is considered medically necessary for the following indications when accompanied by pain and functional disability (interference with ADLs) (see also Additional Note ): Aseptic loosening of one or more prosthetic components confirmed by imaging; or Fracture of one or more components of the prosthesis or worn or dislocated plastic insert confirmed by imaging; or Confirmed periprosthetic infection by gram stain and culture (Note: A single stage revision is considered medically necessary for this indication, unless there has been a prior infection in the same joint, in which case a multi-stage revision may be considered medically necessary); or Periprosthetic fracture of distal femur, proximal tibia or patella confirmed by imaging; or Progressive or substantial periprosthetic bone loss confirmed by imaging; or Bearing surface wear leading to symptomatic synovitis; or Implant or knee malalignment (valgus/varus or flexion/extension greater than 15 degrees); or Knee arthrofibrosis; or Instability or dislocation of the TKA; or Extensor mechanism instability; And member does not have any of the following contraindications to total knee revision surgery: Poor bone quality; or Highly limited quadriceps or extensor function; or Poor skin coverage; or Poor vascular status. Unicompartmental knee arthroplasty using Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved devices is considered medically necessary for members with advanced osteoarthritis or post-traumatic arthritis of the knee affecting only a single compartment (medial, lateral or patellofemoral), and who meet the following criteria (see also Additional Note ): Pain and functional disability that interferes with ADLs due to osteoarthritis or post-traumatic arthritis of the knee joint; and Limited range of motion, crepitus, or effusion or swelling of knee joint on physical examination: and Member must have intact, stable ligaments, in particular the anterior cruciate ligament; and Patient’s knee arc of motion (full extension to full flexion) is not limited to 90 degrees or less; and Radiographic evidence of moderate/severe osteoarthritis (i.e., Kellgren-Lawrence Grade 3 or 4) (see Appendix ) affecting only a single (medial, lateral or patellofemoral) compartment of the knee joint; and History of of unsuccessful conservative therapy (non-surgical medical management; 12 or 24 weeks depending on age/BMI) that is clearly addressed in the medical record (see Note Footnote3 *** ) with at least half of the necessary conservative therapy consisting of formal physical therapy (in-person with a licensed physical therapist as opposed to home or virtual physical therapy). Physical therapy needs to be confirmed either by the actual PT notes, or by documentation in the member claims history. Conservative therapy may be inappropriate for severe osteoarthritis with bone-on-bone articulation in the weight-bearing portion of the joint (medial and/or lateral but not patello-femoral); and Footnote3 *** Note: Conservative therapy includes all of the following, unless contraindicated: Anti-inflammatory medications or analgesics; and Flexibility and muscle strengthening exercises; and Activity modification; and Supervised physical therapy (activities of daily living [ADLs] diminished despite completing a plan of care); and Assistive device use (required for persons with relative contraindications Footnote4 † to joint replacement, optional for others); and Therapeutic injections into the knee (required for persons with relative contraindications Footnote4 † to joint replacement, optional for others). Footnote4 † Relative contraindications to joint replacement include the following: morbid obesity (BMI greater than 40), age less than 50 years). Members with relative contraindications should exhaust all nonsurgical treatment options. Member has none of the following contraindications to unicompartmental knee arthroplasty: Previous proximal tibial osteotomy or distal femoral osteotomy; or Tibial or femoral shaft deformity; or Radiographic evidence of medial or lateral subluxation; or Flexion contracture greater than 15 degrees; or Varus deformity greater than 15 degrees (medial unicompartmental knee arthroplasty) or a valgus deformity greater than 20 degrees (lateral unicompartmental knee arthroplasty); or Inflammatory or crystalline arthropathy; or Subchondral bone loss due to large subchondral cysts or extensive focal osteonecrosis. Member has none of the following absolute contraindications to joint replacement: Active infection of the joint or active systemic bacteremia that has not been totally eradicated; or Active skin infection (exception recurrent cutaneous staph infections) or open wound within the planned surgical site of the knee; or Corticosteroid injection into the joint within 12 weeks of the planned arthroplasty; or Vascular insufficiency, significant muscular atrophy of the leg, or neuromuscular disease severe enough to compromise implant stability or post-operative recovery or quadriplegia; or Osseous abnormalities that cannot be optimally managed and which would increase the likelihood of a poor surgical outcome (i.e., inadequate bone stock to support the implant); or Allergy to components of the implant (e.g., cobalt, chromium or alumina). For members with significant conditions or co-morbidities, the risk/benefit of unicompartmental knee arthroplasty should be appropriately addressed in the medical record. Prophylactic use of tranexamic acid is considered medically necessary in total knee arthroplasty to decrease blood loss. Note : Intra-operative use of kinetic balance sensor for implant stability during knee replacement arthroplasty is considered incidental to the primary procedure being performed and is not eligible for separate reimbursement. Additional Note If member is diabetic, their hemoglobin A1C (HbA1c) should be less than 8 percent within 3 months prior to knee arthroplasty. Experimental, Investigational, or Unproven The following are considered experimental, investigational, or unproven because their effectiveness has not been established: Bacteriophage therapy for the treatment of knee arthroplasty-related peri-prosthetic joint infection Bicompartmental, staged bicompartmental, and bi-unicompartmental knee arthroplasty for osteoarthritis of the knee and all other indications Custom instrumentation for the procedure including cutting blocks Customized total or partial knee implant Genicular nerve radiofrequency ablation for peri-operative pain control in total knee arthroplasty (TKA) and treatment of chronic pain in well-appearing TKA Mineralized collagen-enhanced bone cement for total knee arthroplasty Prophylactic radiation therapy following total knee arthroplasty “Smart Knee Implants” (e.g. Zimmer Persona IQ) Tele-rehabilitation after TKA UniSpacer inter-positional spacer for the treatment of osteoarthritis affecting the medial compartment of the knee; Augmented or virtual reality (AR/VR) assistance for knee art

results.snippet: These researchers retrospectively reviewed 84 patients (100 knees) with bicompartmental UKA and 71 patients (77 knees) with medial UKA/PFA. Clinical and radiographical evaluations were performed at a minimum follow-up of 5 years (mean of 12 years; range of 5 to 23 years). Bicompartmental arthroplasty reliably alleviated pain and improved function. Prosthesis survivorship at 17 years was 78 % in the bicompartmental UKA group and 54 % in the medial UKA/PFA group. The high revision rate, compared with TKA, may be related to several factors such as implant design, patient selection, crude or absent instrumentation, or component mal-alignment, which can all contribute to the relatively high failure rate in this series.

    "Patient’s knee arc of motion (full extension to full flexion) is not limited to 90 degrees or less; and",
    "Radiographic evidence of moderate/severe osteoarthritis (i.e., Kellgren-Lawrence Grade 3 or 4) (see Appendix) affecting only a single (medial, lateral or patellofemoral) compartment of the knee joint; and",
    "History of of unsuccessful conservative therapy (non-surgical medical management; 12 or 24 weeks depending on age/BMI) that is clearly addressed in the medical record (see Note Footnote3 ***) with at least half of the necessary conservative therapy consisting of formal physical therapy (in-person with a licensed physical therapist as opposed to home or virtual physical therapy).
